summary: An experimental document that takes a broad look at distributed printing and lists real-life scenarios that clarify the features needed in an Internet printing protocol. It identifies requirements for end users, operators and administrators.

eli5.summary: Before building a way to print over the internet, the designers wrote down who would use it and what each person needs.

subtitle: What people printing over the Internet need, written down before the protocol itself.

tldr.problem: Printing across the Internet needs more than a local printer protocol: users must find printers, install drivers, submit jobs, check status and cancel, possibly across firewalls and organizations.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists goals for three roles (end user, operator, administrator), sets objectives such as security, extensibility and firewall traversal, and walks through scenarios like discovery, job submission and notification. Only a subset of end-user goals is meant for IPP/1.0.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental requirements document, one of a set that together describe the Internet Printing Protocol; the IESG expected a revised standards-track protocol to follow.

sections.title: Where This Document Fits
sections.content:
This is one of a set of documents that together describe the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP), an application level protocol for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies. IPP is heavily influenced by the printing model of the Document Printing Application (DPA) standard. DPA covers end-user and administrative features, but IPP/1.0 focuses only on end-user functionality.

The set includes the rationale document (RFC 2568), the encoding and transport document (RFC 2565), the mapping between LPD and IPP (RFC 2569), the model and semantics document and an implementer's guide. The IESG note on this memo warns that the standards-track version is expected to differ, in particular by adding strong authentication and privacy features and an ipp: URL type.
sections.eli5: This is the first page of a big plan for printing over the Internet. It explains what the plan is for before the details are written.

sections.title: Terminology and Printer Configurations
sections.content:
Internet printing means using Internet tools to print to a remote printer with the same methods and operations as for a local or local-area-network printer, after initial setup. A printer is any device that can mark on media. A driver is the code in the client operating system that produces the print data stream; how drivers are installed is operating system dependent and outside the scope of IPP.

Three physical configurations are supported: a client talking to a Printer object embedded in one device; a client talking to a server holding one or more Printer objects, each tied to one physical device; and a client talking to a Printer object that stands for one or more physical devices. In every case the protocol between server and device is undefined, and the end user sees a single device.
sections.eli5: A printer can be one machine, or a helper computer in front of one or many machines. Either way, the person sees just one printer.

sections.title: Design Goals by Role
sections.content:
For the end user, the memo lists finding a printer (by name, location or capability), creating a local instance of it, viewing printer status and capabilities, submitting a job, viewing job status and canceling a job. Jobs can come from an application, as a file pushed from the user's computer, or by reference to a document at a URI that is resolved before printing. The protocol must support job-to-printer capability matching, though not every implementation has to provide it. Parameters such as number of copies, single or two sided printing, finishing and job priority can be set at submission. Users need status and notification when a job completes, and the creator of a job must be able to cancel it or its remaining portion. Altering a job is not a V1.0 goal.

The operator monitors printers, replenishes supplies, clears minor errors and re-prioritizes jobs, and needs alerts such as out of paper. The administrator creates printer instances, manages lists of authorized users, operators and administrators, and handles billing. Both roles are marked as not required for V1.0.
sections.eli5: A person who prints wants to find a printer, send a page, see how it is going and stop it if needed. Helpers who fix the printer and bosses who run it come later.

sections.title: Objectives of the Protocol
sections.content:
The protocol must be independent of the operating system of both client and server, and must handle both on-the-fly print data (as in Windows 95, Windows NT and OS/2) and spooled data (as typical in UNIX) without the user noticing. A web browser or server is not required.

  • Extensibility: a process to register new attributes and enumerated values with IANA, syntax for private attributes, and versioning and negotiation so later versions can interoperate with version 1.0.
  • Firewalls: printing between enterprises is supported, so the protocol must pass through firewalls and proxy servers where the administrator allows it, preferably without changing firewall technology.
  • Internationalization: enabled where appropriate.
  • LPD: no backward compatibility with LPD (RFC 1179) is required, but a mapping must be provided so a gateway can be built.
sections.eli5: The plan must work on any computer, let new features be added later, get past a company's safety gate, and work for people around the world.

sections.title: Scenarios
sections.content:
Section 5 sketches six scenarios as protocol-neutral flows: printer discovery through a directory service, driver installation, submitting a print job, getting status or capabilities, asynchronous notification and job canceling. Not all of the functions shown are assumed to be in IPP/1.0.

Submitting a job must support three sources of data: a file submitted with the job, data generated on the fly, and a file referenced by a URI. Every request gets a response, such as that the job was queued, is printing, failed with a reason, or could not be printed. The protocol must also handle overrun in the printer and support overlapped printing and downloading in devices that cannot spool. The appendix expands these into detailed scenarios, from discovery within one enterprise to end-to-end printing across the Internet.
sections.eli5: The document acts out stories: find a printer, send a page, ask how it is going, get a message when it is done, or cancel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IPP is required to work in a secure environment and, wherever reasonable, should reuse existing protocols such as SSL3 and HTTP Digest Access Authentication (RFC 2069) rather than invent new ones. It must work with different mechanisms and policies because the threats vary. Two considerations drive this: the client, the Printer and the document may each sit in different security domains, and the sensitivity of the content varies, for instance a payroll document versus a public one. Message protection goals include data origin authentication, privacy, integrity and non-repudiation.

Downloading and installing a driver exposes a computer to defective, malicious or inappropriate software. Administrators should configure driver downloads so the source can be verified and the software protected in transit.
sections.eli5: Printing secret papers needs locks, and you should only install helper programs from places you can check.
